title: Joey Jordison
text:
Joseph James Jordison, better known as Joey Jordison, was an American musician, primarily known as the drummer for the heavy metal band Slipknot. He was born on December 17, 1975, in Des Moines, Iowa, to Karen and Mark Jordison. His early life was relatively quiet, spent in the suburban area of West Des Moines. He began playing drums at the age of nine, initially inspired by drummers like Neil Peart of Rush and John Bonham of Led Zeppelin. He built his first drum kit from spare parts, demonstrating a natural aptitude and dedication to the instrument.

Jordison's musical journey began in the early 1990s with several local bands, including the progressive metal group Modifidious, formed in 1993. This band, featuring future Slipknot members Paul Gray and Shawn "Clown" Crahan, provided an important formative experience, honing his technical skills and fostering his collaborative spirit. They released a demo tape in 1995, showcasing a burgeoning talent and a willingness to experiment with different musical styles. Jordison’s drumming was already displaying a complexity and power that would become hallmarks of his later work.

The pivotal moment in Jordison’s career arrived in 1995 when he was invited to join Slipknot, initially as a temporary replacement. The band, conceived by Shawn Crahan and Paul Gray, was already developing a distinctive and aggressive sound, drawing influences from bands like Metallica, Obituary, and Fear Factory. Jordison’s audition proved successful, and he became a permanent member, taking on the number one designation within the band's masked persona system. 

Slipknot's self-titled debut album, released in 1999, catapulted them to international fame. Jordison’s drumming on the album, characterized by its intricate rhythms, double bass proficiency, and sheer intensity, was a key factor in its success. The album sold over 6 million copies worldwide and earned a Grammy Award for Best Metal Performance in 2000 for the song “Wait and Bleed.” Jordison's contribution wasn’t limited to simply playing the drums; he also co-wrote several songs, showcasing his growing compositional skills. 

Throughout Slipknot’s career, Jordison remained a crucial creative force. He contributed significantly to subsequent albums, including *Iowa* (2001), *Vol. 3: (The Subliminal Verses)* (2004), *All Hope Is Gone* (2008), and *.5: The Gray Chapter* (2014). He also played a significant role in the band’s elaborate stage shows, known for their chaotic energy and theatrical elements.  In 2011, Jordison began playing bass guitar on Slipknot tracks, demonstrating further versatility.  He also contributed to the soundtrack for the film *Gears of War 3* in 2011.

Beyond his work with Slipknot, Jordison pursued other musical projects. He formed the thrash metal supergroup Scar the Martyr in 2013 with members of Mudvayne and Bueler. The band released a self-titled debut album in 2014, earning positive reviews for its aggressive sound and technical musicianship. He also participated in the band Northman, formed in 2015, blending heavy metal with folk music influences.

In August 2013, Jordison announced his departure from Slipknot, citing "personal reasons." While the specifics of his departure remained largely private for several years, he later revealed in 2016 that he had been diagnosed with acute transverse myelitis, a rare autoimmune disease that affected his nervous system and significantly impacted his ability to play the drums.  He stated the condition made it impossible for him to continue touring with the band.

Despite the challenges posed by his illness, Jordison remained active in music. He continued to work on various projects and collaborated with other artists. He worked on the soundtrack for the video game *Doom Eternal* in 2020, contributing drumming and bass tracks. 

Joey Jordison passed away on July 28, 2021, at his home in Urbandale, Iowa, at the age of 45. His death was announced by Slipknot, who expressed their profound sadness and acknowledged his immense contribution to the band’s legacy. A private funeral service was held in Des Moines, attended by close friends and family.  His death was attributed to an undiagnosed artery ailment. Jordison is survived by his fiancée, Stefanie Ramaeker, and his parents, Karen and Mark Jordison. His influence on the drumming world, particularly within the heavy metal genre, remains undeniable, and he is remembered as a fiercely talented and innovative musician.

title: Diego Suarez (garden designer)
text:
Diego Suarez, a prominent figure in contemporary garden design, was born on July 12, 1968, in Rosario, Argentina. His early life was deeply influenced by the region’s fertile soil and vibrant flora. Rosario, a major port city on the Paraná River, boasts extensive parks and gardens, and Suarez’s parents, both amateur botanists, instilled in him a fascination with plants and their cultivation. He spent much of his childhood exploring local nurseries and assisting his parents in their own small backyard garden, developing a keen eye for form, texture, and colour combinations.

Suarez's formal education began at the Escuela de Arte Mariano Moreno in Rosario, where he initially studied fine arts, intending to pursue painting. However, a mandatory course in landscape architecture during his second year proved to be a pivotal turning point. He discovered a natural aptitude for spatial design and a desire to work directly with the natural world, quickly shifting his focus. He graduated with a degree in Landscape Architecture in 1992, a period marked by a growing interest in sustainable practices and ecological design principles.

Following graduation, Suarez worked briefly for a local landscape construction firm, gaining practical experience in installation and project management. However, he felt constrained by the purely functional nature of the work. In 1994, he made the decision to move to London, United Kingdom, seeking opportunities to develop his design skills and engage with the more experimental and diverse landscape architecture scene. He secured a position as a junior designer at Arne Maynard Associates, a highly respected firm known for its historically-informed and meticulously detailed English garden designs. Maynard became a significant mentor, teaching Suarez the importance of rigorous research, a deep understanding of plant heritage, and the creation of spaces that felt both timeless and deeply rooted in their context.

Suarez remained at Arne Maynard Associates for nearly eight years, steadily progressing to the role of senior designer. During this time, he contributed to numerous prestigious projects, including the restoration of the walled garden at Heligan Estate in Cornwall (completed in 1999), a project which garnered considerable acclaim.  He also worked on private gardens across the UK and Europe, developing a signature style characterized by a harmonious blend of formal structure and naturalistic planting.

In 2002, Suarez established his own practice, Diego Suarez Garden Design, based in London. The firm quickly gained a reputation for creating bespoke gardens that were both visually stunning and ecologically sound. His early commissions included the redesign of a courtyard garden in Chelsea for a prominent art collector (completed in 2003) and the creation of a rooftop garden for a luxury apartment building in Canary Wharf (2005). 

Suarez's work began to receive wider recognition in 2008 when he won a Gold Medal at the RHS Hampton Court Palace Flower Show for his garden, "The Hidden Retreat," a design that showcased the potential of small urban spaces to provide tranquil escapes and support biodiversity. This victory significantly boosted his profile and led to an influx of new clients. Since then, his designs have appeared in numerous publications, including *The World of Interiors*, *House & Garden*, and *Gardens Illustrated*. He has designed over 150 private gardens, ranging in size from small urban courtyards to sprawling country estates.  His portfolio also includes several public spaces, including the redesign of a community garden in Hackney, London (2012), and the planting scheme for a new park in Bristol (2017).

A consistent theme throughout Suarez’s career has been his commitment to sustainable design. He prioritizes the use of native plants, drought-tolerant species, and organic gardening practices. He also actively incorporates rainwater harvesting systems and composting programs into his designs whenever possible. He has lectured extensively on sustainable landscape design at universities and horticultural societies across Europe, advocating for a more ecologically responsible approach to garden creation.

In 2021, Suarez published his first book, *Designing with Nature: A Contemporary Approach to Garden Design*, which explores his design philosophy and showcases a selection of his most notable projects.  He currently resides in Oxfordshire with his wife, a botanist, and continues to lead Diego Suarez Garden Design, taking on a limited number of projects each year to maintain the quality and personalized attention that defines his work. As of 2023, his firm employs a team of five designers and horticulturalists.  Suarez remains a highly sought-after garden designer, known for his meticulous attention to detail, his innovative use of plant material, and his unwavering commitment to creating beautiful and sustainable outdoor spaces.

title: Daniel Alexander Cameron

He specialized in civil litigation, representing businesses and individuals in a variety of legal disputes. His work included handling cases involving contracts, torts, and commercial law.  During his time at Frost Brown Todd, Cameron also became increasingly involved in Republican politics. He served as chairman of the Jefferson County Republican Party from 2015 to 2019. This position involved leading the local party organization, fundraising, and mobilizing volunteers for Republican candidates. He was a vocal supporter of Donald Trump during the 2016 and 2020 presidential campaigns, frequently speaking at rallies and events.

Cameron’s political career took a significant turn in 2019 when he announced his candidacy for Kentucky Attorney General. He secured the Republican nomination in May 2019, defeating two other candidates.  In the November 2019 general election, Cameron defeated Democratic incumbent Andy Beshear, who was running for governor, with 57.9% of the vote to Beshear’s 41.9%. Cameron was sworn into office on January 6, 2020, becoming the first African American to hold the position of Kentucky Attorney General.

As Attorney General, Cameron focused on issues such as combating drug trafficking, protecting vulnerable populations, and upholding the rule of law.  He launched several initiatives targeting opioid abuse, including lawsuits against pharmaceutical companies and efforts to increase access to addiction treatment. He also prioritized prosecuting cases involving child abuse and elder fraud. One notable case involved investigating allegations of improper spending by the University of Louisville Foundation, which resulted in settlements and policy changes.  In 2020, Cameron gained national attention for his handling of the Breonna Taylor case, a shooting involving a Black woman who was fatally shot by Louisville police officers. While he presented evidence to a grand jury, no officers were initially charged directly with Taylor’s death, leading to protests and criticism. He later secured an indictment of a former Louisville police officer, Brett Hankison, on charges of wanton endangerment.

In 2023, Cameron announced his candidacy for the Republican nomination for Governor of Kentucky. He won the nomination in May 2023, defeating several other contenders, including former UN Ambassador Kelly Craft. He faced incumbent Democratic Governor Andy Beshear in the November 2023 general election. Beshear won re-election, securing 52.5% of the vote to Cameron’s 47.5%. The election was considered close, with a margin of approximately 78,000 votes. 

Following his defeat, Cameron returned to his legal practice. He is married to Connie Cameron (née Branch), and they have two children.  He remains an active figure in Kentucky Republican politics, and his future political aspirations are subject to speculation. He is 44 years old as of November 2024, and continues to reside in Louisville, Kentucky.

title: Jeremy Corbyn

Jeremy Bernard Corbyn was born on October 26, 1949, in Newport, Wales, to Vera (née Osborne), a textile engineer, and David Corbyn, a Dominican-born electrical engineer. His parents, both politically active, were members of the Communist Party of Great Britain, and their activism heavily influenced Corbyn's early life. The family moved to Highbury, North London, in 1959, where Jeremy attended William Parker School and then Hazelwood School. He has described feeling like an outsider during his schooling, largely due to his socialist beliefs and opposition to the prevailing conservative attitudes. He left school at 18 without completing A-levels, a decision he later said he regretted.

Following his departure from formal education, Corbyn travelled extensively, initially in Tunisia and Libya, where he volunteered with agricultural projects assisting local communities. These experiences solidified his commitment to social justice and international solidarity. He returned to London in 1970 and became involved in local politics, working for the National Union of Public Service Librarians (NUPSL) as a union representative. He began his political career in the Labour Party, initially supporting the Trotskyist Socialist Labour League. However, he joined the Labour Party in 1975.

Corbyn first contested Parliament as a candidate for Labour in Bristol South in 1983, finishing third with 13,736 votes. He stood again in Birmingham Northfield in 1987, achieving a slightly better result but still failing to win. His breakthrough came in 1997 when he was elected as the Member of Parliament (MP) for Islington North, a constituency he has represented ever since. He secured 53% of the vote, a comfortable majority.

Throughout his parliamentary career, Corbyn consistently advocated for policies aligned with the left wing of the Labour Party. He was known for his strong opposition to military intervention, particularly the 2003 invasion of Iraq, which he vocally condemned. He frequently raised concerns about social inequality, poverty, and the arms trade in Parliament. He served on various committees including the Select Committee on International Development from 1997 to 2001 and the Standards Committee from 2005 to 2008.

Corbyn’s profile rose significantly in the lead-up to the 2015 Labour leadership election following the resignation of Ed Miliband. He initially entered the contest as a relatively unknown figure, but his anti-establishment message and calls for a more socially just and egalitarian society resonated with a broad swathe of the party membership and registered supporters. He gained substantial momentum through online campaigning and grassroots support. Despite being initially dismissed by many within the parliamentary Labour Party, he ultimately secured a surprising 30% of first-preference votes in the first round.

In the second round, he continued to gain support, eventually winning the leadership election on September – 12, 2015, with 59.8% of the votes in the second round, defeating Andy Burnham and Yvette Cooper. This victory marked a significant shift within the Labour Party and reflected a surge in grassroots activism.

As leader, Corbyn struggled to unite the party and faced considerable challenges, including divisions over Brexit and persistent criticism from within his own parliamentary colleagues. He maintained a focus on social justice issues, advocating for policies such as increased public spending, renationalisation of key industries, and stronger international cooperation. He led the Labour Party in two general elections, achieving a result of 40% of the vote in 2017 and 32.1% in 2019. Despite gaining seats in 2017, the party ultimately lost ground in 2019.

Corbyn resigned as Labour leader on October 29, 2019, following the disappointing general election result. He formally stepped down as an MP on March 29, 2020. Since leaving Parliament, he has remained involved in public life, focusing on campaigning for peace and social justice through organizations like Stop the War Coalition, of which he has been a long-time supporter. He has also spoken out on issues such as climate change and international solidarity. He remains a prominent figure within the left wing of the political landscape, continuing to advocate for the policies and values he has championed throughout his career.

title: Gemma Arterton
text:
Gemma Christina Arterton was born on February 2, 1986, in Gravesend, Kent, England. Her mother, Sally Patrick, is a nurse, and her father, Barry Arterton, is a retired IT consultant. She has two older brothers, Mark and George. Arterton’s upbringing was relatively ordinary; she attended Wilmington Grammar School for Girls, a state secondary school, and demonstrated an early interest in performing arts. She began taking dance classes at the age of three, initially in tap, then progressing to ballet, contemporary, and jazz. By the age of 15, she was attending the Gravesend Dance & Drama Academy, honing her skills and gaining experience in stage productions.

Arterton’s professional journey began in 2003 when she landed a role in a touring production of *Abraham Lincoln: Vampire Hunter*, a significant early experience that allowed her to travel and perform across the UK. Following this, she joined the National Youth Music Theatre, participating in several productions between 2003 and 2005. A pivotal moment arrived in 2007 when she was cast as Lisa Sparks in the BBC mini-series *Mar & Mrs. Smith*, a British adaptation of the popular film. This role brought her wider recognition and marked her television debut.

Her film career truly began to take off in 2008. She gained considerable attention for her portrayal of Elspeth Marlowe in *Quantum of Solace*, the 22nd film in the James Bond franchise, released in November 2008. This was followed quickly by a starring role in *St Trinian’s* (2009), a comedic film where she played the character of Charlie Buller. The success of *St Trinian’s* led to a sequel, *St Trinian’s 2: The Legend of Fritton’s Gold*, in 2009, further solidifying her presence in British cinema.

The late 2000s and early 2010s saw Arterton taking on a wider range of roles, demonstrating her versatility. She appeared in Woody Allen’s *You Will Meet a Tall Dark Stranger* (2010), alongside Antonio Banderas and Naomi Watts, and played Titania in a critically acclaimed stage production of *A Midsummer Night's Dream* at the Globe Theatre in 2013. This Shakespearean role showcased her classical acting abilities and garnered significant praise. In 2014, she starred in *Hansel & Gretel: Witch Hunters*, a fantasy action film, and played the lead role in *To Kill a King*, a historical drama about the assassination of Kaiser Wilhelm II.

Arterton continued to build her career with diverse projects. She played Gemma Bennett in the ITV drama *The Tunnel* (2013-2016), a complex and challenging role that demonstrated her dramatic range. In 2018, she starred in *Their Finest*, a charming and poignant film about women working in the British film industry during World War II, earning her a BAFTA nomination for Best Actress in a Supporting Role. She also appeared in *Summerland* (2020), a moving drama set during World War II, and *The King’s Man* (2021), the first installment in a prequel series to the *Kingsman* film franchise.

Beyond acting, Arterton has been a vocal advocate for gender equality and body positivity. She has spoken openly about the pressures faced by women in the film industry and has championed more diverse representation on screen. She has also been involved in initiatives promoting the arts and supporting young performers. In 2018, she co-founded ReFrame, a campaign advocating for greater gender parity in the film industry.

In 2019, Arterton married Freddie Porter, a London-based businessman. They have two children, a son born in 2021 and a daughter born in 2023. While maintaining a busy acting schedule, Arterton has also expressed a keen interest in directing, having directed short films and music videos. As of 2024, she continues to work steadily in film and television, demonstrating a consistent and impressive career trajectory spanning over fifteen years, with a total of approximately 40 film and television credits. Her estimated net worth is around $10 million, reflecting her success and enduring popularity.

title: Shin Jea-hwan
text:
Shin Jea-hwan, born Shin In-seok on February 28, 1917, in Haeju, Hwanghae Province, Korea (then under Japanese colonial rule), was a pivotal figure in the development of Korean modern poetry. He is recognized as a leading voice of the “Second Generation” of Korean poets, a group that emerged in the 1940s and sought to break away from the earlier, more overtly patriotic and romantic styles. Shin Jea-hwan’s work is characterized by its exploration of existential themes, psychological depth, and a distinctive use of imagery drawn from everyday life and the natural world.

Shin’s early life was marked by political unrest and the growing influence of Japanese colonialism. He attended Haeju Middle School and later, in 1934, entered Keijo Imperial University (now Seoul National University) to study Japanese Literature. It was during this period that he began to seriously engage with poetry, initially influenced by Japanese modernist poets like Ishikawa Takuboku. He adopted the pen name Shin Jea-hwan, reportedly to distance himself from his family’s conservative background. He became involved with a literary society called “Seongsin-hoe” (New Mind Society), which was a forum for discussing literature and Korean independence. In 1938, he was expelled from Keijo Imperial University for his involvement in anti-Japanese student demonstrations, a common occurrence for Korean intellectuals during that era.

Following his expulsion, Shin worked various jobs, including as a journalist for the *Dong-A Ilbo* newspaper, though he was frequently dismissed due to his outspoken views. He continued to write poetry, and in 1943, his first collection, *Ojokgyeongui Chueok* (The Tracks of the Lonely), was published. This collection, though small, established him as a significant new voice in Korean poetry, immediately recognizable for its introspective tone and rejection of conventional poetic forms. The collection was printed in only 500 copies due to the wartime restrictions imposed by the Japanese authorities.

The liberation of Korea in 1945 brought a period of significant political and social upheaval. Shin continued to publish poetry, and in 1946, he co-founded the literary journal *Hyundae Munhak* (Modern Literature), which became a vital platform for new and experimental writing. He served as editor-in-chief for a considerable period. During the Korean War (1950-1953), Shin was forced to flee Seoul as North Korean forces advanced. He spent several years living in Busan, the temporary capital of South Korea, while the war raged. This experience deeply impacted his writing, adding a layer of sorrow and displacement to his already introspective style.

Shin Jea-hwan’s most celebrated work is considered to be *Yeongyeongui Haneul* (The Sky of Youth), published in 1954. This collection, reflecting on the losses and anxieties of the Korean War, solidified his reputation as one of the nation’s most important poets.  He received numerous awards throughout his career, including the Tonghui Literary Award in 1962 and the Korea Literary Award in 1986. He held various academic positions, including professor of Korean literature at Seoul National University from 1964 until his retirement in 1987. He published several more collections of poetry, including *Gureumui Siseo* (Through the Rain) in 1968 and *Bicheurim* (The Reflection of a Tree) in 1982. His complete poems were compiled and published in 1995, running to over 800 pages.

Shin Jea-hwan’s contribution to Korean literature extends beyond his own poetry. He was a dedicated teacher and mentor to younger poets, and his literary criticism helped shape the understanding and appreciation of modern Korean poetry. He was known for his rigorous intellectual honesty and his commitment to artistic integrity. He married Kim Ok-ja in 1948, and they had two children, a son and a daughter. Shin Jea-hwan died on January 17, 1996, at the age of 78, in Seoul, South Korea. His legacy as a profound and influential poet continues to resonate within Korean literary circles, and his works are studied and celebrated for their enduring exploration of the human condition.

title: Nuh Omar
text:
Nuh Omar Hussein, often referred to simply as Nuh Omar, was a pivotal figure in the development of modern Somali literature and a prominent intellectual and politician in Somalia's formative years. Born on December 19, 1902, in Beledweyne, then part of British Somaliland, his early life was shaped by the complexities of colonial rule and the burgeoning Somali nationalist sentiment. His father, Hussein Mohamed, was a respected elder and traditional leader within the Majeerteen clan, and his mother, Faduma Farah, came from a lineage known for its oral storytelling traditions. This combination fostered both a deep understanding of Somali culture and a nascent awareness of the need for its preservation and advancement.

Omar’s formal education began in 1917 at the Italian-run school in Mogadishu, then under Italian colonial control. This was a relatively rare opportunity for Somali children at the time. He quickly demonstrated an aptitude for languages, mastering Italian and later Arabic. He remained in Mogadishu, completing his education and subsequently working as a translator for the Italian colonial administration from 1922 to 1928. This role exposed him to a wider world and provided valuable insights into colonial governance, which he would later critique. In 1928, he moved to Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, seeking further religious education and broadening his linguistic skills. He spent several years studying Arabic and Islamic jurisprudence, returning to Mogadishu in 1934.

Upon his return, Nuh Omar began his literary career. Recognizing the importance of written Somali, he dedicated himself to standardizing the language and promoting its use in literature and journalism. Prior to this, Somali was primarily an oral language, with limited written material. He co-founded *Ururka Isbahaysiga Ummaddeena* (The Somali National Unity Society) in 1935, a key organization in the early Somali nationalist movement. This society aimed to unite Somalis across colonial boundaries and advocate for greater self-governance. He also began publishing poetry and short stories in the *Al-Fatat* newspaper, a publication he helped establish. His writing, characterized by its elegant prose and socially conscious themes, quickly gained popularity. He wrote extensively about Somali culture, history, and the injustices of colonial rule, often using poetic allegory to circumvent censorship.

During World War II, British forces occupied Mogadishu. Omar, initially cooperating with the British administration due to the Italian collapse, became increasingly critical of their policies. He was briefly imprisoned in 1943 for his outspoken criticism, further solidifying his image as a nationalist leader. Following the war, he continued his political activism, participating in the 1947 British-sponsored Somali Political Union, a coalition of Somali nationalist groups advocating for Somali unification. He played a crucial role in drafting the union’s constitution.

With Somalia’s independence from Italy in 1960, Nuh Omar entered politics. He served as Minister of Education from 1960 to 1962, a period dedicated to developing a national education system and promoting Somali language and culture. He spearheaded the creation of the National Institute of Somali Language and Literature, aimed at standardizing the Somali language and producing educational materials. He also advocated for the inclusion of Somali history and culture in the school curriculum. He briefly served as Minister of Interior in 1964.

However, his political career was cut short by the 1969 coup led by Siad Barre.  Omar, along with other prominent politicians, was arrested and placed under house arrest. He remained under surveillance for years, effectively silenced from public life. While not publicly executed like many other political opponents of the Barre regime, he lived under strict restrictions and faced significant hardship.

Despite the suppression, Nuh Omar continued to write, albeit secretly. His literary works, particularly his poetry collections *Biyo Dhulka Soo Galay* (Water Reaching the Land) and *Qaar Qalbiigayga Dhex Yaal* (Things in My Heart), remain highly regarded as masterpieces of Somali literature. He is credited with writing over 300 poems, numerous short stories, and several essays on Somali culture and politics. 

After the collapse of the Siad Barre regime in 1991, Nuh Omar re-emerged as a respected elder and intellectual, though his health was failing. He lived a quiet life in Mogadishu, occasionally offering counsel to political leaders. He died on October 21, 1993, at the age of 90, leaving behind a significant legacy as a literary pioneer, nationalist leader, and champion of Somali language and culture. His contributions are considered instrumental in shaping modern Somali identity and literature.

title: Jeff Long (athletic director)
text:
Jeffrey Long was born on February 15, 1960, in Little Rock, Arkansas, to James and Patricia Long. He grew up in the city, attending Catholic High School where he excelled as a linebacker and earned all-state honors. Long’s early life instilled in him a strong connection to Arkansas and a passion for athletics. He attended the University of Arkansas in Fayetteville, graduating in 1982 with a Bachelor of Arts degree in marketing. While at Arkansas, he served as student body president, demonstrating early leadership qualities and an ability to connect with a diverse student population. He also participated in the Razorback Marching Band, playing the trombone.

Long's professional career began immediately after graduation in 1982, joining the University of Arkansas athletic department as an assistant athletics director for development. His initial role focused on fundraising and donor relations, a skill set that would prove crucial throughout his career. He quickly ascended the ranks, becoming Associate Athletics Director in 1987, responsible for development, marketing, and special events. During this period, he played a significant role in increasing donations to the Razorback athletic program, contributing to facility improvements and enhanced student-athlete support.

In 1993, Long transitioned to the University of Pittsburgh, joining the staff of Athletic Director Carl S. Kraus. He served as the Assistant Athletic Director for Development, again focusing on fundraising and donor cultivation. He remained at Pittsburgh for five years, gaining valuable experience in a larger, more complex athletic program. In 1998, he returned to Arkansas, this time as the Executive Associate Athletics Director. This position saw him take on increasing responsibility for the day-to-day operations of the athletic department, working closely with then-Athletic Director Frank Broyles.

A pivotal moment arrived on April 17, 2008, when Long was named the Athletic Director at the University of Arkansas. He succeeded Frank Broyles, who had served in the position for a remarkable 35 years. At 48 years old, Long was tasked with leading one of the nation’s premier athletic programs, navigating the evolving landscape of college athletics, and maintaining the Razorbacks' tradition of excellence.

During his tenure as Athletic Director, Long oversaw significant achievements. He secured a lucrative television contract with the Southeastern Conference (SEC), ensuring substantial revenue for the athletic department. He also championed facility upgrades, including renovations to Donald W. Reynolds Razorback Stadium, the construction of the R.W. Johnson Coliseum, and improvements to athletic training facilities.  Under his leadership, Arkansas teams achieved considerable success across various sports. The football team reached the Cotton Bowl Classic in 2010, the Sugar Bowl in 2011, and the Texas Bowl in 2012. The men's basketball team made several NCAA Tournament appearances, including an Elite Eight run in 2015.  The women's basketball program also achieved consistent success, reaching the NCAA Tournament numerous times. Long prioritized academic achievement among student-athletes, consistently maintaining high graduation rates.  He was known for his calm demeanor and his ability to build strong relationships with coaches, donors, and university administrators.

Long resigned as Athletic Director on April 17, 2022, after 14 years in the position.  He cited a desire to spend more time with his family as the primary reason for his departure.  His resignation coincided with increasing scrutiny surrounding the athletic department's handling of a Title IX complaint involving a former volleyball coach.  While he maintained his innocence regarding any wrongdoing, the situation contributed to his decision to step down.

Following his departure from Arkansas, Long briefly served as a consultant for collegiate athletic programs. He also remained involved in community activities in Northwest Arkansas.  He and his wife, Kim, reside in Fayetteville, Arkansas.  They have three children – Brooke, Justin, and Landon – and several grandchildren.  Jeff Long’s career is marked by a dedication to Arkansas athletics, a focus on fundraising and development, and a commitment to the success of student-athletes both on and off the field.

title: José Hernández Delgadillo
text:
José Hernández Delgadillo, often simply referred to as José Hernández, is a prominent Mexican-American astronaut, engineer, and author. His journey from a migrant worker’s son to a NASA astronaut embodies the American dream and serves as an inspiration to countless individuals, particularly those from underserved communities. He was born on August 7, 1966, in Stockton, California, the youngest of five children to migrant farmworkers José Hernández and María del Refugio Delgadillo. His parents, originally from Guadalupe, Zacatecas, Mexico, moved frequently throughout California and Washington, following seasonal agricultural work, picking crops like asparagus, strawberries, and apples.

Growing up, Hernández’s family lived in various temporary dwellings, including labor camps and borrowed housing, often moving every few months. Despite the challenges of a transient lifestyle and limited access to educational resources, Hernández’s parents instilled in him a strong work ethic and a commitment to education. They emphasized the importance of hard work and encouraged their children to pursue their dreams, famously telling José, “Sí, se puede,” meaning “Yes, you can,” a phrase that became his personal mantra and a rallying cry for his career.

He attended schools in Ripon, California, and later graduated from Ripon High School in 1984. He then pursued higher education, earning a Bachelor of Science degree in Electrical Engineering from Santa Clara University in 1986. Following graduation, he joined Rockwell International, initially working as an electrical engineer on the Space Shuttle program, specifically contributing to the design and testing of the Shuttle’s electrical power systems. This role provided him with a foundational understanding of space technology and fueled his ambition to be more than just an engineer supporting the program.

In 1989, Hernández joined NASA as a general engineer at the Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. He initially worked on mission support, focusing on electrical systems and robotics. He steadily progressed within the organization, gaining experience in diverse areas of space exploration. In 2004, after 15 years of dedicated service and rigorous training, Hernández was selected as one of fourteen astronauts in the NASA Astronaut Candidate Program. He underwent intensive training, including survival training, Russian language courses, and spacecraft systems instruction. He received his astronaut training at the Yuri Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center in Star City, Russia.

His first and only spaceflight occurred in August s 2009, aboard Space Shuttle Discovery’s STS-128 mission. As a mission specialist, he was responsible for operating the robotic arm, performing tasks related to the installation and maintenance of the International Space Station (ISS). The mission, which lasted from August 27 to September 11, 2009, involved the delivery of the U.S. laboratory module, Columbus, and other critical equipment to the ISS. During the 13-day mission, the crew completed 179 orbits of Earth and traveled a total of 5.8 million miles. Hernández became the first Mexican-born astronaut to travel to space.

Following his spaceflight, Hernández remained involved with NASA, serving as an astronaut and CAPCOM (Capsule Communicator), a crucial role where he communicated directly with astronauts in space. He retired from NASA in 2011. Since then, he has dedicated his time to inspiring young people to pursue careers in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). He frequently visits schools and gives motivational speeches, sharing his story and emphasizing the importance of education and perseverance.

In 2012, Hernández published his autobiography, “To the Stars and Back: Journeys Beyond the Horizon,” which details his life story, from his humble beginnings as a migrant worker’s son to his journey to space. The book has been widely praised for its inspiring message and has become a staple in many schools and libraries. He has since released a children's version of the book and has continued to advocate for STEM education and opportunities for underrepresented communities. He now serves on several boards and committees dedicated to education and outreach.  He resides in Houston, Texas, with his wife, Adela, and their four children. José Hernández continues to be a powerful symbol of what can be achieved through dedication, hard work, and the belief in oneself, demonstrating that the sky is truly the limit.

title: Sandra Pisani

Sandra Pisani was born on March 12, 1942, in Valletta, Malta, the only child of Joseph and Tessie (née Borg) Pisani. Her father, Joseph Pisani, was a prominent Maltese lawyer and politician, eventually serving as Speaker of the Maltese Parliament from 1969 to 1976. Her mother, Tessie, was a homemaker and active in local charitable organizations. Growing up in a politically engaged household, Sandra was exposed to discussions of law, governance, and social issues from a young age. She received her early education at the Sacred Heart Convent School in Valletta, demonstrating a keen intellect and a strong aptitude for languages.

After completing her secondary education, Sandra pursued higher education, initially studying law at the University of Malta. She graduated with a Bachelor of Laws degree in 1964, a significant achievement for a woman in Malta at that time, where female participation in the legal profession was still limited. Following her undergraduate studies, she traveled to London, England, to further her education. In 1966, she obtained a Master of Laws degree from the University of London, specializing in international law. This postgraduate degree solidified her expertise and broadened her understanding of legal systems beyond the Maltese context.

Returning to Malta, Sandra Pisani was admitted to the Maltese Bar in 1967 and commenced practice as a lawyer. She quickly established a reputation for meticulous preparation, sharp legal arguments, and a commitment to her clients. Unlike many of her male counterparts who focused on corporate or high-profile criminal cases, Sandra initially built her practice around representing individuals in family law and civil litigation. She was known for her empathetic approach, particularly in sensitive cases involving divorce, custody disputes, and inheritance matters.

In c. 1976, a pivotal moment arrived in Sandra’s career. She was appointed as a magistrate in the Maltese court system, becoming one of the first women to hold such a judicial position in Malta. This appointment was a landmark decision, signifying a growing recognition of women’s capabilities within the Maltese legal and governmental structures. She served as a magistrate for over two decades, presiding over a wide range of cases, from petty crimes to more serious offenses. She consistently demonstrated fairness, impartiality, and a deep understanding of the law. Her tenure as magistrate was marked by a reputation for efficiency and a willingness to adapt to evolving legal principles.

Beyond her judicial duties, Sandra Pisani became a vocal advocate for women’s rights and gender equality in Malta. She actively participated in organizations promoting women's advancement and contributed to discussions surrounding legislative reforms aimed at improving the legal status of women. She frequently spoke at conferences and seminars, advocating for equal opportunities in education, employment, and the legal system. She believed strongly in the importance of mentorship, informally guiding and encouraging young women pursuing careers in law and other traditionally male-dominated fields.

Sandra Pisani retired from her judicial duties in 2000, after nearly 24 years of service. Following her retirement, she remained active in public life, continuing to contribute to legal scholarship and participate in discussions on social issues. She served on various committees and boards, offering her expertise on legal and ethical matters. She also dedicated time to supporting charitable organizations, reflecting her lifelong commitment to community service.

In 2014, she was appointed as Malta’s Ambassador to the Vatican, a prestigious and highly symbolic role. This appointment recognized her distinguished career and her commitment to representing Malta on the international stage. She served as Ambassador to the Vatican until 2018, representing Malta with dignity and professionalism.

Sandra Pisani passed away on April 21, 2023, at the age of 81. Her death was met with widespread tributes from the Maltese legal community, government officials, and the wider public, who acknowledged her pioneering role in the Maltese legal system, her advocacy for women’s rights, and her dedication to public service. She left behind a legacy of integrity, fairness, and a commitment to justice that continues to inspire generations of Maltese lawyers and citizens.

title: Sami Shalom Chetrit
text:
Sami Shalom Chetrit was born on December 23, 1953, in Taza, Morocco, to a Jewish family of Moroccan-Spanish origin. His parents, Rachel and Isaac Chetrit, were both educators. Taza, at the time, was a town with a significant Jewish community, and Sami’s early childhood was shaped by this cultural environment, steeped in Sephardic traditions and Judeo-Arabic language. He received his initial education in the local Alliance Israélite Universelle school, a network of Jewish schools established throughout the diaspora. In 1965, at the age of 12, his family immigrated to Israel, settling in the Tel Aviv suburb of Holon.

The move to Israel proved transformative, requiring him to learn Hebrew and adapt to a new educational system. He attended the Holon High School, where he excelled in his studies, demonstrating a particular aptitude for languages and history. He began to explore his Sephardic heritage more deeply, recognizing the marginalization of Sephardic Jewish culture within Israeli society. This awareness would become a defining theme of his academic and activist work.

Chetrit began his university studies at Tel Aviv University in 1971, earning a Bachelor's degree in History and Middle Eastern Studies in 1975. He continued his education at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, completing a Master's degree in 1978, focusing on the history of Moroccan Jews during the French Protectorate. He then pursued a doctorate at the University of California, Berkeley, receiving his Ph.D. in History in 1985. His doctoral dissertation, "The Jews of Morocco under French Rule: Settlement, Politics and Identity, 1912-1956," became a seminal work in the field, providing a nuanced and critical analysis of the colonial experience of Moroccan Jews.

Upon returning to Israel, Chetrit joined the faculty of Tel Aviv University, initially as a lecturer and eventually becoming a full professor in the Department of Middle Eastern Studies. He has held numerous visiting professorships at universities worldwide, including the University of California, Berkeley, Harvard University, and Columbia University, reflecting the international recognition of his scholarship.

Chetrit’s academic work has focused primarily on the history and culture of Sephardic Jews, particularly those of Moroccan origin, within the broader context of North African Jewish communities and the Israeli state. He is renowned for his interdisciplinary approach, combining historical analysis with insights from anthropology, sociology, and literary studies. He has authored and edited numerous books and articles, translated into several languages. Key publications include “The Jews of Morocco under French Rule” (1990), “Moroccan Jews: A History” (2016), and “Beyond Mizrahi: Jewish Identity and Cultural Difference in Israel” (2019).

Beyond his academic contributions, Chetrit has been a vocal and influential advocate for the recognition and inclusion of Mizrahi Jewish culture within Israeli society. He has consistently challenged dominant narratives that prioritize Ashkenazi Jewish experiences and perspectives, arguing for a more equitable and inclusive understanding of Israeli history and identity. He has been involved in various public debates and initiatives aimed at promoting Mizrahi cultural expression and addressing issues of social and economic inequality.  He co-founded the “Mizrahi Forum,” a platform for dialogue and advocacy concerning Mizrahi Jewish issues, and has served on advisory boards for cultural organizations and governmental committees.

Throughout his career, Chetrit has received numerous awards and honors for his scholarship and activism, including the Bernstein Award for Jewish History in 2017. He has been recognized for his contributions to understanding the complexities of Jewish identity in the modern world and for his tireless efforts to promote social justice and cultural understanding.  As of 2023, he continues to teach and conduct research at Tel Aviv University, remaining a leading voice in the study of Sephardic Jewish history and a prominent figure in Israeli public life. He is married to Shoshana Gavish, and they have two children.

title: Jackie Shroff
text:
Jagdeep Jagannath Shroff, known professionally as Jackie Shroff, was born on December 1, 1957, in Bombay (now Mumbai), India. His father, Jagannath Shroff, was a businessman involved in textiles, and his mother, Geeta Shroff, was a teacher. He hails from a family with roots in Khoram, a village in the Valsad district of Gujarat. She received numerous accolades, including three Screen Actors Guild Award nominations for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Comedy Series (2014, 2015, and 2016). The show ran for seven seasons, concluding on July 26, 2019, and Polanco’s presence remained a consistent and vital element throughout.

Beyond *Orange is the New Black*, Polanco has steadily built her acting resume. She appeared in the film *Ben-Hur* (2016), a reimagining of the classic biblical epic, portraying a supporting role. She also had a recurring role in the television series *Rosewood* (2017-2018), playing the character of Isabella Vega. In 2019, she starred in the independent film *Lost Girls*, a true crime drama based on the disappearance of Shannan Gilbert. More recently, she had a role in the Netflix film *Uncorked* (2020) and appeared in the series *The Guilty* (2021).

Polanco is an advocate for several causes, including immigrant rights and education. She has used her platform to raise awareness about the challenges faced by Dominican communities and to encourage young people to pursue their dreams despite obstacles. She has partnered with organizations like the Hispanic Scholarship Fund, supporting educational opportunities for Latino students.

In her personal life, Polanco has been open about her struggles with body image and self-esteem. She has become a vocal proponent of body positivity and encourages others to embrace their individuality. She has two sons, Avery and Bastian, whom she prioritizes in her life. She maintains a relatively private personal life, focusing on her family and career. As of 2023, she is actively pursuing new acting opportunities and continues to advocate for causes she believes in, demonstrating a commitment to both her craft and social responsibility. Her estimated net worth is around $4 million, largely accumulated through her work on *Orange is the New Black* and subsequent acting roles.

title: Joseph Kony
text:
Joseph Kony, born on April 12, 1964, in Odek, a village in Gulu District, northern Uganda, is a Ugandan rebel leader most infamous for his command of the Lord’s Resistance Army (LRA). His life has been marked by a brutal insurgency that spanned decades, leaving a trail of devastation across Uganda, South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and the Central African Republic.

Kony’s early life was relatively unremarkable. He was born to a peasant family and received limited formal education, attending a local primary school before dropping out. He was reportedly a charismatic figure, although described by some as initially unremarkable, and displayed an ambition that would later manifest in a violent and destructive manner. He joined the Uganda People's Defence Force (UPDF) in the late 1980s, but was reportedly dismissed for insubordination, fueling a resentment that would later contribute to his rebellion.

The LRA was formally established in 1988, initially claiming to fight against the government of President Yoweri Museveni, alleging corruption and marginalization of the Acholi people, an ethnic group prevalent in northern Uganda. Kony, drawing on local spiritual beliefs and manipulating traditional Acholi customs, quickly rose to prominence as the movement's leader. He presented himself as a messianic figure, claiming divine guidance and promising to establish a theocratic state based on the Ten Commandments. This messaging, combined with the promise of food and protection, attracted a large number of child soldiers, a defining characteristic of the LRA.

The LRA’s insurgency escalated rapidly. From 1988 until the early 2000s, the group perpetrated widespread atrocities, including massacres of civilians, abduction of children for use as soldiers and sex slaves, and the mutilation of victims. Estimates of the death toll attributed to the LRA range from 100,000 to over 400,000. Hundreds of thousands more were displaced from their homes, creating a humanitarian crisis in the region. The LRA’s tactics were notoriously brutal, with widespread reports of forced marriages, sexual violence, and the use of children in combat roles.  Kony’s leadership style was autocratic and cult-like; he demanded absolute obedience and enforced his will through fear and violence.

Despite numerous attempts by the Ugandan government and regional forces, Kony and the LRA proved remarkably resilient. In the early 2000s, the LRA shifted its operations eastward, crossing into South Sudan and subsequently into the Democratic Republic of Congo in 2004.  This expansion further complicated the conflict and broadened the scope of the humanitarian crisis.  The Ugandan military pursued the LRA across these borders, often with the support of neighboring countries.

In 2005, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued arrest warrants for Kony and several of his top commanders, including Vincent Otti, for crimes against humanity and war crimes, including murder, rape, and the forced recruitment of child soldiers. Otti, Kony’s second-in-command for many years, was reportedly killed by Kony in 2007, though this was initially denied by Kony.  The ICC’s involvement significantly increased international pressure on Kony and the LRA.

The Ugandan government, with support from the United States and other nations, launched Operation Light-Up Northern Uganda in 2011, a military operation aimed at capturing Kony.  The African Union deployed the Regional Task Force (RTF) in 2011, comprised of troops from Uganda, South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Central African Republic, to pursue the LRA. Despite these efforts, Kony remained elusive, operating primarily in the dense jungles of the Central African Republic and the Democratic Republic of Congo.  The LRA’s strength diminished significantly over the years, with many fighters defecting or being killed.

As of 2020, Kony was believed to be hiding in the remote areas of the Central African Republic, with a dwindling number of followers, estimated to be fewer than 100. He has not been seen publicly since 2014.  The United States government offered a reward of $7 million for information leading to his arrest.  While the LRA's immediate threat to regional stability has subsided, the legacy of Kony's reign of terror continues to impact the communities affected by the conflict, with ongoing efforts focused on supporting displaced populations, reintegrating former child soldiers, and addressing the long-term trauma caused by the insurgency.

title: Alfred Hitchcock
text:
Alfred Hitchcock, born Alfred Joseph Hitchcock on August 13, 1899, in Leytonstone, Essex, England, was arguably the most influential and recognizable film director in cinematic history. His career spanned over six decades, producing 53 feature films and numerous short films, television productions, and theatrical pieces. His innovative techniques, masterful storytelling, and signature blend of suspense, horror, and dark humor earned him the moniker “The Master of Suspense.”

Hitchcock’s childhood was marked by a stern Catholic upbringing and a separation from his parents, particularly his mother, Emily, for extended periods. This early experience, he later claimed, contributed to his anxieties and a sense of abandonment which he explored thematically in many of his films. He attended St. Ignatius College, a Jesuit school in London, and subsequently studied engineering at London University. However, his passion lay in art and design. In 1922, he began working at Paramount Pictures’ British branch in Shepherd’s Bush, initially as a title card designer. He rapidly ascended through the ranks, becoming an assistant art director and then a script reader. This provided him with invaluable experience in understanding narrative structure and visual storytelling.

His directorial debut came in 1925 with *The Pleasure Garden*, a silent film co-directed with Viggo Larsen. This was followed by *The Lodger: A Story of the London Fog* (1927), a thriller widely considered his first significant success and a landmark in the development of the suspense genre. The film’s innovative use of foreshadowing and psychological tension demonstrated Hitchcock’s burgeoning directorial talent. The late 1920s and early 1930s saw him direct a series of British thrillers including *The Man Who Knew Too Much* (1934), a film he would remake later in his career, and *The 39 Steps* (1935), a classic espionage thriller.

In 1939, Hitchcock accepted an invitation from producer David O. Selznick to relocate to Hollywood and head the British branch of RKO Pictures. He quickly became a major force in American cinema. *Rebecca* (1940), his first American film, won the Academy Award for Best Picture and established him as a leading director in the United States. The 1940s were a particularly fruitful period, with films like *Suspicion* (1941), starring Cary Grant and Joan Fontaine, *Shadow of a Doubt* (1943), and *Notorious* (1946), featuring Cary Grant and Ingrid Bergman, cementing his reputation for psychological suspense. *Spellbound* (1945) was notable for its surreal dream sequence designed by Salvador Dalí.

The 1950s saw Hitchcock continue to produce iconic films. *Strangers on a Train* (1951) explored the disturbing concept of a "barter" for murders. *Rear Window* (1954), starring James Stewart and Grace Kelly, is considered by many to be his masterpiece, showcasing his skill in building suspense within a limited setting. *To Catch a Thief* (1955), another collaboration with Cary Grant and Grace Kelly, was a stylish and sophisticated thriller set on the French Riviera. The 1960s included *Vertigo* (1958), initially a box-office disappointment but now considered a groundbreaking exploration of obsession and identity, and *Psycho* (1960), a groundbreaking horror film that revolutionized the genre and famously featured the shower scene. *The Birds* (1963) demonstrated his ability to create terror from seemingly ordinary natural phenomena.

Throughout the 1970s and 1980s, Hitchcock transitioned to television with *Alfred Hitchcock Presents*, a weekly anthology series that ran from 1955 to 1962 and was revived in later decades. His final theatrical film was *Family Plot* (1976), a somewhat self-referential thriller. He received an honorary Academy Award in 1968 for his lifetime achievements.

Hitchcock’s impact on filmmaking is immeasurable. His techniques, such as the MacGuffin (a plot device that motivates the characters but is ultimately unimportant in itself), subjective camera angles, and meticulous editing, are still studied and emulated today. He married twice: first to Alma Reville in 1926, a partnership that lasted until her death in 1986, and then to Barbara Leon in 1980. Alfred Hitchcock died on April 29, 1980, in Los Angeles, California, at the age of 80, leaving behind a legacy as one of the greatest and most influential filmmakers of all time.

title: Chris John (boxer)
text:
Chris John, born Chris Manusama on March 1, 1984, in Tual, Southeast Maluku, Indonesia, is a retired Indonesian professional boxer widely considered one of his nation’s greatest ever pugilists. His career, spanning over a decade, was largely defined by his dominance in the super featherweight division and his exceptional defensive skills.

John’s early life was steeped in boxing tradition. His father, Manusama John, was a local boxing trainer and introduced Chris to the sport at a very young age. He began training seriously around the age of 10, honing his reflexes and footwork in the modest facilities available in his small hometown. Early amateur competitions were limited, but he quickly gained a reputation for his unusual defensive style and unwavering composure. He participated in the 2002 Asian Amateur Boxing Championships, representing Indonesia, but did not medal. Despite this, his potential was evident, and he turned professional in December 2003, signing with PT. Istora Promotions.

His professional debut occurred on December 12, 2003, against Paulus Puyol in Jakarta, which he won by unanimous decision.  He quickly amassed a winning streak, establishing himself as a rising contender.  By 2006, he was challenging for the vacant World Boxing Organization (WBO) super featherweight title against Adama Traore on February 24, 2006, in Jakarta.  John secured a unanimous decision victory, becoming Indonesia’s first world boxing champion in over two decades. This victory was a monumental moment for Indonesian boxing and generated significant national pride.

John's reign as WBO super featherweight champion was remarkably long and successful. He defended his title a staggering 14 times, a record for an Indonesian boxer.  His defenses were characterized by his exceptional defensive prowess, often frustrating opponents with his elusive movement and ability to absorb punches. Notable defenses included victories over Rachim Hamid (Indonesia) on May 12, 2006, Genaro Hernandez (Mexico) on December 9, 2006,  and Takuma Ganeko (Japan) on June 28, 2008.  His fight against Aurelio Jose Honorato (Argentina) on March 28, 2009, was another significant defense, showcasing his tactical brilliance.  He consistently employed a shoulder roll defense, a technique popularized by Muhammad Ali, to avoid taking significant damage.

Throughout his championship reign, John faced numerous challenges, but his ability to adapt and control the pace of the fight consistently resulted in victory. While sometimes criticized for a lack of aggression, his strategic approach and remarkable durability proved highly effective. His reign was briefly interrupted in 2011 when he relinquished his title, citing health concerns and a desire to spend more time with his family.

He returned to the ring in 2013, competing in a series of non-title bouts, primarily in Indonesia. He faced Daud Yordan, a fellow Indonesian boxer, in a highly anticipated clash on January 19, 2013, losing by unanimous decision. This marked his first professional defeat.  He continued to fight sporadically, seeking to regain his former glory, but his performances lacked the dominance of his championship years.  His final professional fight was against Samsul Tanjung on December 17, 2017, in Jakarta, which he won by unanimous decision.

Chris John officially retired from professional boxing on February 27, 2018, ending a career that spanned 15 years. His record stood at 46 wins (22 by knockout), 2 losses, and 2 draws. His impact on Indonesian boxing is undeniable. He inspired a generation of young boxers and elevated the sport's profile in Indonesia.  He is now involved in coaching and mentoring young aspiring boxers, sharing his knowledge and experience to help cultivate the next generation of Indonesian boxing talent. He remains a revered figure in Indonesian sports, celebrated for his defensive mastery, longevity, and the national pride he brought to the country during his reign as WBO super featherweight champion.

title: David Oyite-Ojok
text:
